questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) What is a molar solution?

(ii) Calculate the mass of $\mathrm{Na_2S_2O_3\cdot5H_2O}$ needed to prepare $250\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of a $0.011\ \mathrm{M}$ solution in a volumetric flask. (RMM = 248) *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A molar solution is a solution that contains **one mole of solute in one cubic decimetre ($1\ \mathrm{dm^3} = 1000\ \mathrm{cm^3}$) of solution**, that is a concentration of $1\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ (1 M). The volume is that of the final solution, not of the solvent added.

**(ii)** Amount of $\mathrm{Na_2S_2O_3\cdot5H_2O}$ required:

$n = c \times V = 0.011\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}} \times \dfrac{250}{1000}\ \mathrm{dm^3} = 2.75\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}$

Mass required:

$m = n \times M = 2.75\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol} \times 248\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}} = 0.682\ \mathrm{g}$

**Mass = 0.68 g** (0.682 g). In practice: weigh 0.682 g of the crystals, dissolve them in a little distilled water in a beaker, transfer quantitatively to the 250 cm$^3$ volumetric flask, rinse the beaker into the flask and make up to the mark with distilled water; stopper and invert to mix.

questions.enonce_markdown: Calculate the percentage yield when $2.30\ \mathrm{g}$ of ethanol reacts completely with excess ethanoic acid to give $3.52\ \mathrm{g}$ of ethyl ethanoate. (RMM: Ethanol = 46; Ethyl ethanoate = 88.0) *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Equation (esterification): $\mathrm{C_2H_5OH} + \mathrm{CH_3COOH} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3COOC_2H_5} + \mathrm{H_2O}$. One mole of ethanol would give one mole of ester.

Amount of ethanol: $n = \dfrac{2.30}{46} = 0.0500\ \mathrm{mol}$.

Theoretical yield of ethyl ethanoate (acid in excess, so ethanol is limiting): $0.0500\ \mathrm{mol} \times 88.0\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}} = 4.40\ \mathrm{g}$.

$\text{percentage yield} = \dfrac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100 = \dfrac{3.52}{4.40} \times 100 = 80.0\ \%$

**Percentage yield = 80 %.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The radioactive decay of ${}^{63}_{28}\mathrm{Ni}$ $\rightarrow$ ${}^{63}_{29}\mathrm{Cu}$ has a half-life of 120 years.

(i) Write the equation for the radioactive decay of nickel

(ii) What do you understand by the half-life of a radioactive isotope?

(iii) Calculate how long it will take for $1.20\ \mathrm{g}$ of nickel to be reduced to $0.15\ \mathrm{g}$ *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The mass number stays at 63 while the atomic number rises from 28 to 29: a neutron has changed into a proton, so this is **beta-minus decay** (an electron and an antineutrino are emitted):

$${}^{63}_{28}\mathrm{Ni} \rightarrow {}^{63}_{29}\mathrm{Cu} + {}^{\ 0}_{-1}\mathrm{e} + \bar{\nu}_e$$

Check: mass number $63 = 63 + 0$; charge $28 = 29 + (-1)$.

**(ii)** The half-life is the **time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample (equivalently, for the activity or the mass of the radioactive isotope) to decay**. It is constant for a given isotope: it does not depend on the amount present or on temperature and pressure.

**(iii)** Number of half-lives: $\dfrac{1.20}{0.15} = 8 = 2^3$, so the mass has been halved **3 times** ($1.20 \rightarrow 0.60 \rightarrow 0.30 \rightarrow 0.15\ \mathrm{g}$).

$t = 3 \times t_{1/2} = 3 \times 120\ \text{years} = 360\ \text{years}$

**Time = 360 years.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The nitride ion ($\mathrm{N^{3-}}$), the oxide ion ($\mathrm{O^{2-}}$) and the aluminum ion ($\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$) are isoelectronic.

(i) Why are they considered to be isoelectronic?

(ii) Arrange the above ions in order of increasing ionic size beginning with the smallest size. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Ions (or atoms) are isoelectronic when they have the **same number of electrons and the same electronic configuration**. Here:

- $\mathrm{N^{3-}}$: $7 + 3 = 10$ electrons
- $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$: $8 + 2 = 10$ electrons
- $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$: $13 - 3 = 10$ electrons

All three have the configuration $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6$ (that of neon).

**(ii)** The three ions have the same number of electrons and the same number of shells, so the size depends on the nuclear charge: the larger the number of protons, the more strongly the 10 electrons are pulled in and the smaller the ion (nuclear charge $+13 > +8 > +7$).

**Order of increasing ionic size: $\mathrm{Al^{3+}} < \mathrm{O^{2-}} < \mathrm{N^{3-}}$.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The data below is for the kinetic study of the reaction: $\mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{C} + \mathrm{D}$

| Concentration of A / mol dm$^{-3}$ | 0.58 | 0.40 | 0.28 | 0.20 | 0.14 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Time / $10^2$ s | 4 | 8 | 12 | 16 | 20 |

(i) What is meant by the terms "order of reaction" and "instantaneous rate" as used in chemical kinetics?

(A) Order of reaction:

(B) Instantaneous reaction rate:

(ii) From the data, determine the half-life of the reaction.

(iii) Determine the order of reaction with respect to A. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)(A) Order of reaction.** For a rate equation $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^m[\mathrm{B}]^n$, the order with respect to A is the **power $m$ to which the concentration of A is raised in the experimentally determined rate equation** (it shows how the rate depends on $[\mathrm{A}]$); the overall order is the sum $m + n$. It is found by experiment, not from the balanced equation.

**(B) Instantaneous rate.** It is the **rate of reaction at one particular instant**: the rate of change of concentration at a given time, equal to the **gradient of the tangent** to the concentration-time curve at that time (unlike the average rate, which is taken over a whole time interval).

**(ii) Half-life.** The half-life is the time for the concentration of A to fall to half of a given value. The times are $4, 8, 12, 16, 20 \times 10^2\ \mathrm{s}$, that is $400, 800, 1200, 1600, 2000\ \mathrm{s}$.

- $0.40 \rightarrow 0.20\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$: from $800\ \mathrm{s}$ to $1600\ \mathrm{s}$, so $t_{1/2} = 800\ \mathrm{s}$.
- $0.28 \rightarrow 0.14\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$: from $1200\ \mathrm{s}$ to $2000\ \mathrm{s}$, so $t_{1/2} = 800\ \mathrm{s}$.
- $0.58 \rightarrow 0.29\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$: from $400\ \mathrm{s}$ to about $1170\ \mathrm{s}$ (interpolating between 0.40 at 800 s and 0.28 at 1200 s), so about $770\ \mathrm{s}$, which agrees with $800\ \mathrm{s}$ within the accuracy of the reading.

**Half-life $= 800\ \mathrm{s}$ ($8\times10^2\ \mathrm{s}$).**

**(iii) Order with respect to A.** The half-life is **constant (800 s) whatever the starting concentration** (0.40, 0.28 or 0.58 mol dm$^{-3}$). This is the characteristic of a **first-order** reaction. Check: the concentration drops by the same factor in each equal interval of 400 s ($0.58/0.40 = 1.45$, $0.40/0.28 = 1.43$, $0.28/0.20 = 1.40$, $0.20/0.14 = 1.43$).

**The reaction is first order with respect to A**, with $k = \dfrac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{800\ \mathrm{s}} = 8.7\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$. (The concentration of B is not given, so nothing can be said about the order with respect to B.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Define an acid according to Bronsted and Lowry.

(ii) Phenolphthalein indicator represented by HIn, is a weak acid that dissociates in water as follows:

$\mathrm{HIn(aq)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H^+(aq)} + \mathrm{In^-(aq)}$

HIn is colourless, $\mathrm{In^-}$ is red in colour.

Explain the colour change observed at the end point of an acid-base titration where phenolphthalein is used as indicator with the acid in the conical flask.

(iii) The pH range of phenolphthalein is 8.2 - 10.0. Give an acid and an alkali for which phenolphthalein is suitable as an indicator during titration

(iv) The $\mathrm{OH^-}$ ion concentration in a dilute ammonia solution is $0.0025\ \mathrm{M}$. Calculate the pH of the solutions *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A Brønsted-Lowry acid is a **proton ($\mathrm{H^+}$) donor**, for example $\mathrm{HCl} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_3O^+} + \mathrm{Cl^-}$.

**(ii)** The indicator is in equilibrium: $\mathrm{HIn} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H^+} + \mathrm{In^-}$ (colourless $\rightleftharpoons$ red).

- With the **acid in the conical flask**, the solution contains an excess of $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions: by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium lies on the left, mostly undissociated HIn, so the solution is **colourless**.
- The alkali is run in from the burette. At the end point, the first drop of excess alkali supplies $\mathrm{OH^-}$ ions which remove $\mathrm{H^+}$ ($\mathrm{H^+} + \mathrm{OH^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_2O}$). The equilibrium shifts to the **right** to replace the $\mathrm{H^+}$ used, so $[\mathrm{In^-}]$ builds up and the solution turns **pink/red**.
- The end point is therefore a sharp change from **colourless to pink (red)**.

**(iii)** Phenolphthalein changes colour between pH 8.2 and 10.0, so it is suitable when the pH at the equivalence point (the steep part of the titration curve) lies in that range, which is the case for:

- a **strong acid and a strong base**, for example hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide (the vertical part of the curve spans about pH 3 to 11), and
- a **weak acid and a strong base**, for example ethanoic acid and sodium hydroxide (equivalence-point pH about 8.7 to 9).

It is not suitable for a weak base titrated with a strong acid (equivalence point below pH 7).

**(iv)** $\mathrm{pOH} = -\log_{10}[\mathrm{OH^-}] = -\log_{10}(0.0025) = 2.60$

At 25 $^\circ$C, $\mathrm{pH} + \mathrm{pOH} = 14$ (from $K_w = 1.0\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{mol^2\,dm^{-6}}$), so

$\mathrm{pH} = 14 - 2.60 = 11.40$

**pH = 11.4.**
